questions.question: What low-temperature structural change did the authors associate with the displacement of Na⁺ in droplets of at least 200 water molecules?

options.A: A tetrahedrally ordered low-density core surrounded by a denser, more disordered subsurface
options.B: A uniformly dense core surrounded by a low-density surface shell
options.C: A liquid-like core with ions concentrated at the vapor interface
options.D: A crystalline surface layer surrounding an amorphous, high-density core

questions.rationale: At 200 K the larger droplets develop a low-density tetrahedral core and high-density subsurface; Na⁺ favors that more disordered subsurface rather than the core.
questions.evidence_quote: a lowdensity core with relatively good tetrahedral ordering 31 is surrounded by a high density subsurface.

questions.question: Which comparison best captures the single-Na⁺ radial distribution at 300 K versus 200 K for droplets with N ≥ 200?

options.A: At 300 K it is nearly uniform in the interior; at 200 K its peak lies within 0.1 nm of the peak in Voronoi-based water density
options.B: At 300 K it peaks at the COM; at 200 K it becomes uniform throughout the droplet
options.C: At both temperatures it peaks at the vapor interface, but the 200 K peak is narrower
options.D: At 300 K it follows the tetrahedral core; at 200 K it follows the surface number-density maximum

questions.rationale: The simulations show an approximately constant interior ion density at high temperature, whereas at low temperature the ion peak tracks the subsurface peak in ρv(r).
questions.evidence_quote: Rather than being centered at r = 0, the peak of ρ N a (r) is located within 0.1 nm of the peak in ρ v (r) (for N ≥ 200).

questions.question: How was the water-density profile ρv(r) constructed, and what physical distinction did the authors use it to make?

options.A: From Voronoi volumes around oxygen sites; it distinguishes fully surrounded interior/subsurface molecules from low-density surface molecules
options.B: From hydrogen-bond counts per shell; it distinguishes liquid water from vapor by tetrahedral order alone
options.C: From oxygen number density only; it identifies the surface as the region of maximum molecule count
options.D: From dipole moments in each shell; it identifies the core as the region of strongest orientational polarization

questions.rationale: The authors average density from oxygen-site Voronoi volumes, which become large at the surface; this allows them to identify surface molecules separately from fully surrounded ones.
questions.evidence_quote: Surface molecules can be identified as those located where ρ v (r) is small, and molecules in the subsurface as those located an intermolecular distance below the point at which ρ v (r) has decayed to near zero.

questions.question: Which limitation did the authors identify for interpreting the ion distribution in the smallest, N=100 droplet at 200 K?

options.A: It lacks a tetrahedrally organized core and has large relative shape fluctuations, with Na⁺ often one or two layers inward from the surface
options.B: It equilibrates too rapidly for the ion density to be measured and always places Na⁺ at the COM
options.C: Its core density is so high that the ion is excluded to the vapor phase
options.D: It contains too few ions for the one-ion distribution to be computed

questions.rationale: The smallest droplet does not form the low-density tetrahedral core characteristic of larger supercooled droplets; shape fluctuations are relatively large and Na⁺ tends to reside near the surface.
questions.evidence_quote: The cluster of N = 100 does not show a tetrahedrally organized core. It is noted that this smaller cluster is subject to larger relative shape fluctuations than the larger droplets.

questions.question: What equilibration check was used for the N=776, 200 K single-ion simulations initialized with Na⁺ at different locations?

options.A: They compared runs initialized at/near the COM and at the surface, finding radial ion densities converged after 400 ns
options.B: They compared runs at 200 K and 300 K and considered them equilibrated once the temperatures matched
options.C: They initiated all ions at the surface and judged equilibration by the number of evaporated waters
options.D: They compared Na⁺ trajectories in different force fields and stopped after 400 ps

questions.rationale: To test equilibration, they started independent simulations with Na⁺ near the center or surface and used convergence of radial ion densities; for N=776 convergence occurred after 400 ns.
questions.evidence_quote: For example, for N = 776 after 400 ns, the ion densities as a function of radial distance from the droplet COM ρ ion (r) converge for the two simulations.

questions.question: What simulation model and integration settings were used for the aqueous droplets?

options.A: TIP4P/2005 water, OPLS-AA Na⁺, Nosé–Hoover thermostat with 0.1 ps time constant, and 2 fs leap-frog steps
options.B: SPC/E water, AMBER Na⁺, Langevin thermostat with 2 fs time constant, and 0.1 ps velocity-Verlet steps
options.C: TIP3P water, OPLS-AA Na⁺, Berendsen thermostat with 2 ps time constant, and 1 fs leap-frog steps
options.D: TIP4P/2005 water, CHARMM Na⁺, microcanonical dynamics, and 0.5 fs Brownian steps

questions.rationale: The methods specify TIP4P/2005 water, OPLS-AA sodium, Nosé–Hoover temperature control, and leap-frog integration at 2 fs.
questions.evidence_quote: The temperature is controlled by using the Nosé-Hoover thermostat with time constant 0.1 ps. The equations of motion are integrated with the leap-frog algorithm with a time step of 2 fs.

questions.question: What does the paper's electrostatic-confinement model predict for a single ion, and under what conditions is this effect more pronounced?

options.A: A harmonic potential centered at the droplet COM, enhanced by low temperature, high charge, small radius, and intermediate dielectric constant
options.B: A repulsive potential centered at the surface, enhanced by high temperature, low charge, and large radius
options.C: A constant potential independent of ion position, enhanced only when the dielectric constant approaches infinity
options.D: A harmonic potential centered at the droplet surface, enhanced by low charge and large radius

questions.rationale: The model assigns a COM-centered harmonic potential and predicts greater electrostatic confinement at low temperature, high charge, small radius, and intermediate dielectric constant.
questions.evidence_quote: Analyzing Eqs. ( 2) and (4) we conclude that the effect will be more pronounced at low temperature, high charge, small radius and intermediate values of the dielectric constant.

questions.question: For five Na⁺ ions in the 776-water droplet at 300 K, how did simulation profiles compare with the paper's nonlinear Poisson–Boltzmann reference?

options.A: The fitted decay length was about 1.2 nm, while using water dielectric constant 75 gave about 0.8 nm; the authors treated the comparison qualitatively because shape fluctuations matter
options.B: The fitted decay length was 0.8 nm, matching the 1.2 nm prediction exactly and validating a rigid-sphere model quantitatively
options.C: The simulation showed no radial decay, whereas the model predicted a 1.2 nm decay length independent of droplet size
options.D: The model predicted 1.3 nm for 776 waters and simulations gave 0.42 nm, which the authors attributed to ion pairing

questions.rationale: For five ions in 776 waters at 300 K the fitted exponential has λPB≈1.2 nm, compared with ≈0.8 nm from ε=75; significant shape fluctuations led the authors to caution against quantitative interpretation.
questions.evidence_quote: For 776 H 2 O molecules -5 Na + ions at T = 300 K the distribution decays (toward the droplet's COM) as an exponential function fitted by 0.42 exp(-(1.14 -x)/1.2), where λ P B ≈ 1.2 nm.

questions.question: What two-peak structure appeared for eight Na⁺ ions in the 1100-water droplet at 200 K, and how did the authors interpret it?

options.A: Peaks at 0.52 and 1.5 nm; the inner lower-intensity peak represents one ion exchanging with ions contributing to the outer peak, not a metastable state
options.B: Peaks at 0.52 and 1.5 nm; the inner peak was assigned to a permanently trapped ion and a metastable intermediate
options.C: Peaks at 1.2 and 1.3 nm; they were attributed to a rigid-sphere Poisson–Boltzmann double layer
options.D: Peaks at 0 and 3.8 nm; they corresponded to the ion in the core and at the droplet surface, respectively

questions.rationale: The two observed maxima were at 0.52 and 1.5 nm; exchange of the single ion associated with the inner peak precludes interpreting the bimodality as metastability.
questions.evidence_quote: In droplets comprising 1100 H 2 O molecules -8 Na + ions two peaks are observed at distance 0.52 nm and at 1.5 nm.

questions.question: Why does the paper conclude that nonlinear Poisson–Boltzmann predictions cannot explain the multiple-ion distribution under supercooling?

options.A: The low-density tetrahedral core expels multiple ions into the disordered subsurface, so the distribution is governed by heterogeneous solvent structure
options.B: The Poisson–Boltzmann model predicts ion evaporation, while simulations prohibit all surface charge
options.C: At supercooling the dielectric constant becomes exactly one, eliminating all electrostatic interactions
options.D: The simulated droplets contain no subsurface layer and therefore violate spherical symmetry

questions.rationale: The authors attribute the failure of the NPB description at low temperature to the tetrahedrally organized low-density core, which shifts multiple ions toward the higher-density, disordered subsurface.
questions.evidence_quote: Because of the manner in which the H 2 O molecules are organized in the droplet's core at supercooling, the distribution of multiple ions cannot be explained by the predictions of the non-linear Poisson-Boltzmann equation.
